# Politics latest: UK to review Chagos deal after Trump criticism
The UK is to review its deal to give the Chagos Islands to Mauritius following stinging criticism by Donald Trump during his meeting with Andy Burnham yesterday. Meanwhile, Burnham hit out at Russia in his UN speech overnight. Follow for updates.

3 hour ago3h ago02:35
## Chagos deal needs US support, defence secretary tells Sky News - after Trump brands it 'terrible'
Andy Burnham will be looking again at the proposed Chagos Islands deal following his meeting with Donald Trump, the defence secretary has confirmed.
When the PM met the US president at the UN General Assembly in New York yesterday, Trump said he did not support the deal and said he thinks "it's terrible" and "ridiculous".
The proposed agreement is to hand over sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the strategically important UK-US Diego Garcia military base through a 99-year lease deal costing as much as £30bn.
Asked this morning whether Burnham will now look again at the deal, Wes Streeting tells Sky News: "Yes.
"This is extremely simple to understand and also fiendishly difficult, which is why successive governments have not reached a conclusion that everyone can live with yet."
**Watch Streeting's answer to Sky's Sophy Ridge below:**
But he says the "simple bit" is that "President Trump does not support this deal", which he says "is material" because the UK needs the US's support for it to work.
The cabinet minister puts it bluntly: "So objectively, in the absence of support from the Americans, is this deal good enough? No. It needs to have the support of the Americans."
Streeting explains: "What we're trying to do here is safeguard one of the most sensitive intelligence and security assets we have anywhere in the world, which is our base in Diego Garcia."
He adds that an interim legal ruling from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) some years ago "created uncertainty about the legal basis of the UK's presence" on the islands, which is considered "a serious risk" which every prime minister since Boris Johnson has felt the need to try and resolve.
**'Going to have to work through detail of US concerns'**
Pushed on whether Burnham will really take on a thorough rethink on the deal, the defence secretary replies: "So what \[Trump\] said yesterday - it wasn't the first time he'd said it, but I think it's a clear indication that is his settled view on the treaty.
"As it stands, we're going to have to work through the detail of the US concerns to get to a point which maybe not everyone will love, but everyone can live with."
Asked if the UK will still cede sovereignty of the islands to Mauritius, Streeting replies: "That's not really been in doubt since we decolonised."
But he adds there is "absolute agreement" between Mauritius, the UK and the US "that we can reach a diplomatic agreement that safeguards the base at Diego Garcia".
The row involves a US-UK military base on the island of Diego GarciaFile pic: AP
17 minute ago17m ago05:51
## Kremlin accuses Burnham of 'stoking anti-Russian sentiment' following speech to UNGA
Andy Burnham has been accused of "fostering an atmosphere of total Russophobia" by the Kremlin.
It follows the prime minister's speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York yesterday, where he took aim at Russian disinformation campaigns against the UK.
Burnham said in his address: "\[Russia has\] used bots and fake websites.
Falsified newspaper articles.
Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC.
They've amplified far right narratives.
And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 General Election."
The PM also accused the Kremlin of seeking to "stoke tensions and unrest", saying they spend £1.3bn a year "on manipulating information".
**Watch: PM announces new plans to tackle hostile attacks**
Now, the Kremlin has responded to Burnham.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Burnham has "said something new".
But he added: "Stoking anti-Russian
sentiment and fostering an atmosphere of total Russophobia is
what Britain is doing.
"And now, ⁠presumably in unison with
Britain, the ​Germans, the French and a number ​of other European
states are doing the ​same thing.
"From our point ⁠of view, this is an utterly short-sighted
policy. It in no way brings us any ⁠closer to any steps that
might, ​in the long term, lead to ​a reduction in tensions and
de-escalation on the European continent."
1 hour ago1h ago04:46
## The Chagos deal is 'hopefully dead' following Burnham's meeting with Trump, say Tories
The deal to hand over sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius is "over now", the Conservatives have said.
It follows US President Donald Trump lambasting the proposals, when he met with Andy Burnham for the first time yesterday.
Reacting to Trump's comments on the deal, Tory deputy leader Alex Burghart tells Sky News: "Hopefully this whole thing is over now.
"We know that the Americans don't want things to change. We know that things can't change without the Americans because they won't change the treaty that they have with us. So hopefully this is done."
He adds: "Hopefully this whole thing is dead. This sort of crazy, crazy plan is over."
**Watch: Streeting says Chagos deal is not good enough**
Burghart is challenged that it was successive Conservative governments that began talks to hand over sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius.
The senior Tory replies: "The... last Conservative foreign secretary was David Cameron. He said, 'we're not doing this... we're not having any more talks about it. These are our islands.'"
But pushed on how he can call the plan "crazy" when it was the Tories who kicked off the negotiations, Burghart insists: "I thought it was a crazy idea all along. The last Conservative foreign secretary said it was a crazy idea, and if Kemi was prime minister now, it wouldn't be happening."
He adds that he thinks it was a mistake for the talks to begin under the Conservatives.
**'This deal should be binned entirely'**
Shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge has also weighed in, saying it "shouldn't have taken another intervention from the president" for Burnham to review the deal.
"If Burnham was really serious about our defence, he would know that this deal should be binned entirely. It is absurd to hand over British sovereign territory, not to mention billions of pounds of hard-pressed taxpayers' money, to an ally of China."
1 hour ago1h ago04:22
## How Trump has changed his position on the Chagos deal
The defence secretary admitted this morning that any deal regarding the sovereignty of the Chagos Islands "needs to have the support of the Americans".
Wes Streeting told Sky News it was clear that the current agreement does not have the White House's backing, saying: "Objectively, in the absence of support from the Americans, is this deal good enough? No."
It follows Donald Trump rubbishing the proposed deal at the United Nations General Assembly yesterday, where he said is a "terrible" agreement and that Andy Burnham "is going to be looking" at it.
But it hasn't always been this way.
The UK government was originally confident they would get the deal ratified because it did once have the backing of their US counterparts, and even at one point, Trump.
There was a time that the president said he'd be "inclined" to back it and said it was "the best" deal available.
So, what's changed - and how has Trump's position evolved?
**Scroll along our timeline to see how we have ended up here...**
Trump Chagos timeline
February 2025
During Sir Keir Starmer's visit to the White House and amid ongoing negotiations over the Chagos Islands, the US president says: "I think we'll be inclined to go along with your country."
22 May 2025
Starmer then signs a deal handing over sovereignty of the Chagos Islands. The agreement includes a 99-year lease on the island of Diego Garcia.
22 May 2025
The same day, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio welcomes the deal, commends the UK and adds: "This agreement secures the long-term, stable, and effective operation of the joint U.S.-UK military facility at Diego Garcia."
20 January 2026
Months later, Donald Trump then calls the deal an "act of great stupidity", an "act of total weakness"and that the islands are being given away for "no reason whatsoever".
5 February 2026
But Trump later rows back and backs the agreement, saying it is "the best he \[Starmer\] could make". He adds that the US "retain\[s\] the right to militarily secure and reinforce the American presence in Diego Garcia".
17 February 2026
The US State Department reaffirms its commitment to the deal, stating: "The US supports the decision of the United Kingdom to proceed with its agreement with Mauritius concerning the Chagos archipelago."
18 February 2026
Trump once again attacks the deal on Truth Social, warning that Starmer "is making a big mistake" and "is losing control of this important Island by claims of entities never known of before".
20 March 2026
Trump criticises the deal in the context of the Iran war, saying: "They didn't want us to use the island \[the US base on Diego Garcia to bomb Iran\], the so-called island, that for some reason they gave up the rights to it."
13 April 2026
Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty confirms to MPs that the Chagos Deal has been put on hold, saying: "The position of the United States president appears to have changed."
1 September 2026
Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran tells MPs that "maintaining long-term operational control and security of the base remains a top priority and is the entire basis for the UK-Mauritius agreement".
22 September 2026
Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Trump says of the deal: "I don't support it. I think it's terrible. It was a terrible deal... And I think the prime minister is going to be looking at \[it\]. It's a very, very strategic location... It's a very important piece of real estate militarily and strategically."
23 September 2026
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting says: "Objectively, in the absence of support from the Americans, is this deal good enough? No. It needs to have the support of the Americans."

2 hour ago2h ago03:43
## UK's Chagos stance shifts amid unshakeable opposition from Trump
There has been a lot of uncertainty hanging over the Chagos deal ever since Donald Trump switched his allegiance from in favour, to dead against.
Today it felt like the government was acknowledging that reality more clearly.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told Sky News that the deal - which would see sovereignty of the Chagos Islands transferred to Mauritius - could not "objectively" be considered a good deal if Donald Trump and the US opposed it.
On that basis, he said the UK would reconsider it - and that effectively, in its current form, the deal couldn't proceed.
Not so long ago, the UK was adamant that this agreement was integral to the security and future of the joint UK-US Diego Garcia military base, and that an interim legal ruling from International Court of Justice (ICJ) over the sovereignty of the islands created uncertainty that was intolerable.
But while Streeting did not backtrack from that position, his argument was that it was effectively redundant given the US position.
That marks a different tone to even 24 hours ago, when defence minister Luke Pollard repeated the line that Trump had previously backed the deal - perhaps to imply that his opposition now might not have merit - or that it could change.
We know the president is famously capricious and changes his mind - but on this it seems he is certain.
Where does that leave Andy Burnham?
The Chagos deal has garnered cross-party opposition in the Commons, so if it is changed substantially, or scrapped entirely, don't expect there to be many tears.
However, that might not stop the prime minister's opponents from portraying this as a capitulation.
But considering Burnham has stressed that this is a deal he inherited from Keir Starmer, perhaps he is happy to wash his hands of it.
**Watch Streeting's interview with Sky's Sophy Ridge here:**
2 hour ago2h ago03:26
## What are the Chagos Islands and what are the terms of the current deal?
The defence secretary has said this morning that the government's Chagos deal is not good enough and requires the support of the Americans.
That's after US President Donald Trump said yesterday that he does not support the deal and thinks "it's terrible" and "ridiculous".
But what is the deal, what's it all about and why does it matter?
**Why are the Chagos Islands so controversial?**
The islands were a dependency of Mauritius when it was a French colony, but the UK claimed them as part of Mauritius in the early 19th century and kept them beyond the country's independence in 1968.
In the early 1970s, the UK expelled everyone from the archipelago, so the US could build a naval base on the biggest island, Diego Garcia.
**Why is the Diego Garcia base so important?**
It is leased to the US but operates as a joint UK-US base and only military employees have been allowed access.
The UK government says its "strategic location" makes it "vital to UK and US power projection in the Indian Ocean and beyond", and it is used to enable a military presence "across the Middle East, Indo-Pacific and Africa".
**Why did the UK agree to return the islands?**
Mauritius and the UK have been in dispute over the Indian Ocean islands for the past 50 years.
In 2010, Mauritius started legal proceedings against the UK and took it to the International Court of Justice in 2018.
In November 2022, the Tory government started sovereignty negotiations with Mauritius, but halted them a year later after a paper by three academics said transferring the islands would be a "major self-inflected blow".
The Labour government picked the talks back up and signed a deal to return the island last May.
Starmer said the UK might otherwise have lost the island over Mauritius's legal claim on the Chagos Islands, which may have allowed hostile countries to set up their own bases or carry out exercises.
**So, what is the final deal?**
- The UK will **hand sovereignty** of the territory over to Mauritius and **lease the Diego Garcia base** from the Mauritian government over 99 years;
- It will **ban other powers** from using the islands around Diego Garcia without agreement with the UK;
- Mauritius will be free to arrange for **resettlement** of Chagossians on all islands except Diego Garcia;
- The period can be extended by a **further 40 years**, if both parties agree;
- The government said the average cost per year is **£101m**. Sky News analysis suggests the total cost could rise as high as £30bn;
- Both the Commons and the Mauritian parliament need to **ratify the deal**.
3 hour ago3h ago03:00
## 'We must help public find way to separate fact from fiction', says minister
Wes Streeting says the government must "help the public to find their way through, to separate fact from fiction" when it comes to information online.
It follows Andy Burnham announcing that the government will create a new National Centre for Information Defence, in his speech to the United Nations General Assembly yesterday.
Asked about how this will work, the defence secretary says: "So we know that there are particularly state actors but also non-state actors that attempt to disrupt our democracy on a daily basis through misinformation and disinformation.
"The challenges around propaganda are an age-old challenge, but they now have a modern relevance and risk because of social media that we've not seen before.
"And in that context, it is really important that we attribute that misinformation, disinformation, where it's happening and also deter it and help the public to find their way through, to separate fact from fiction and to reach their own conclusions about their opinions and how to cast their vote and all of those other things that make this democracy worth defending."
**'This is a new frontier of risk'**
He's also asked about the announcement that the RAF has launched its first ever space squadron this morning, which is dedicated to protecting the UK's satellites.
The defence secretary says this is about tackling "traditional challenges in very modern settings".
"Some of the most sensitive aspects of national security and defence all rely on that technology and space," he adds.
"Just as we're thinking about protecting physical assets here on Earth, we also need to be prepared to defend those assets in space, because this is a new frontier of risk and threat."
